On May 29, 2023, the user asked for a summary of a research-project description about developing formal methods for reasoning in computer science and AI, especially methods applicable to non-classical logics.

The research project described in the user's text aims to control complexity in symbolic reasoning through a modular approach to language, deductive systems, and semantics. It explores partial non-deterministic semantics and multiple-conclusion logical consequence, and seeks to develop CT4L, a public online platform for model checking, satisfiability and validity decisions, proof search, and extracting explanations from proofs. Planned case studies include probabilistic reasoning, information-security proofs, quantum-algorithm correctness, and robustness verification for deep neural networks.

On May 29, 2023, the assistant drafted an approximately 5,000-character project summary in a style inspired by Alan Turing. The project addresses the need for general methods to analyze symbolic reasoning complexity in non-classical logics, including subclassical, paraconsistent, many-valued, and fuzzy logics, which often require case-by-case techniques.

The research project takes a modular approach to studying how a logic’s language, deductive system, and semantics affect reasoning complexity. It builds on research into axiomatization and decision properties of non-classical logics, aiming to develop techniques applicable across a broad range of such logics.

The project explores partial non-deterministic semantics and multiple-conclusion logical consequence. These ideas are intended to support combining the semantics of two logics in a way that captures joining their axiomatizations, updating semantics when new axioms are imposed, and constructing analytic axiomatizations for a given semantics.

The project uses analytic calculi for decision procedures and symbolic proof search. Its multiple-conclusion approach is intended to avoid the added meta-level language associated with alternatives such as sequent calculi, natural deduction, and labelled tableaux, supporting an internal, compositional view of logic and finer tracking of interactions and complexity increases.

The project is developing an online reasoning platform called CT4L, intended to be publicly available. CT4L is meant to connect foundational results with practical needs through case studies and experimentation on real-world examples; the research may later extend to more complex quantified and typed languages.
